Commentary on Surat al-Waqi'a

It is Meccan by consensus among those whose opinion on the exegetes counts. It has been said that it contains verses that are Medinan, or that were revealed during a journey, but all of this is not established. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever persists in reciting Surat al-Waqi'a will never become poor." Also, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may God be pleased with him) invited Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him) to his stipend, but he refused to take it. He was told, "Take it for your dependents," and he said: "They recite Surat al-Waqi'a. I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever recites it will never become poor.'"

The author, Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him), said:

It contains mention of the Resurrection and of the portions of the self in the Hereafter, and understanding this is a wealth with no poverty in it. Whoever understands it occupies himself with preparation.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿When the Event occurs﴾ ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ ﴿abasing and exalting﴾ ﴿when the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ ﴿and the mountains are crumbled into powder﴾ ﴿and become scattered dust﴾ ﴿and you become three kinds﴾ ﴿so the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ ﴿and the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand!﴾ ﴿and the foremost, the foremost﴾ ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Delight﴾.

"Al-Waqi'a" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Sakhkha," "al-Azifa," and "al-Tamma." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both). All of these are names that call for magnifying it and stressing the gravity of its matter. Al-Dahhak said: "al-Waqi'a" is the Blast, which is the blowing into the Trumpet. Some exegetes said: "al-Waqi'a" is the Rock of Jerusalem, which will fall at the Resurrection. All of these are meanings pertaining to the Resurrection.

"Kadhiba" may be a verbal noun, like "al-'Aqiba," "al-'Afiya," and "Khha'inat al-a'yun." The meaning would then be: there is no denial of it, nor any turning back. This is the view of Qatada and al-Hasan. It may also be an adjective for an implied noun, as if He, the Exalted, said: "there is no state of its occurrence that is false." Based on this, the expression may have two meanings: first, "kadhiba" means "that which is denied" regarding what He reported about it, and He called it "kadhiba" for this reason, as you say "a false story," meaning one in which lies are told. Second, "a false state," meaning its occurrence does not fail to happen, as you say: "So-and-so, when he charges, does not turn back."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿abasing and exalting﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: it is abasing and exalting. Al-Hasan, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, and Abu Haywa read "khafidatan rafi'atan" in the accusative, as a state following the state in "there is no denying its occurrence." You may follow the states as you may follow the predicates of a subject. The first reading is more well-known and more eloquent in meaning, because the position of a state in speech is that of something which, if it were not mentioned, one could do without, whereas the position of sentences that the predicate definitively confirms is the position of what matters.

People differed about the meaning of this abasing and exalting in this verse. Qatada and 'Uthman ibn 'Abdullah ibn Suraqa said: the Resurrection abases some peoples to the Fire and exalts other peoples to the Garden. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, and al-Dahhak said: the Blast lowers its voice so that the nearest hears it, and raises it so that the farthest hears it. Most of those who interpreted said: the Resurrection, through the splitting of the heaven, the earth and the mountains, and the collapse of this structure, raises some bodies and lowers others, so it is an expression for the intensity of the terror and turmoil.

The governing element of His saying, the Exalted: "when [it is] shaken" and "occurs" is "occurs," because this is a substitute for the first "when." Some have said that "occurs" is the governing element of the first, because the meaning of the conditional in both is strong, so it is like "whoever" and "whatever" in conditionals, which the verbs after them govern. It has also been said that "when" is annexed to "occurs," so it cannot govern it, and the governing element is an implied verb.

The meaning of "shaken" is: shaken and moved violently. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both). From it comes "the arrow shook in the target" when it trembles after landing. "Rajja" among people is a stirring matter. The lexicographers differed about the meaning of "bussat." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and 'Ikrima said its meaning is: crumbled to bits, as "al-basisa" is ground, which is parched flour, and it is said: "I moistened the flour" when I wet it with water and it remains crumbled. Al-Tabari cited in this:

"Do not bake a baking, nor crumble a crumbling"

This is the saying of a thief whom fear hurried away from the dough, so he said this to his two companions. Some lexicographers said: "bussat" means "was set in motion." They said: "al-khubz" is hard traveling and striking the earth with the hands, and "al-bass" is gentle traveling. They cited the verse:

"Do not bake a baking, nor set in motion a setting in motion, and flank for us Nahshal and 'Abs"

Abu 'Uthman al-Lughawi mentioned this in the book "al-Af'al."

"Al-hab'a" is the fine particles that fly in the air and are hardly seen except in sunlight when it enters through a window. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Qatada said: "al-hab'a" is what flies off from the dryness of plants. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) said: "al-hab'a" is what flies off from the hooves of horses and beasts. Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) also said: "al-hab'a" is what flies off from sparks of fire, and when it is extinguished nothing is found. "Al-munbath" with a three-dotted "th" means: spread throughout all the air. Al-Nakha'i read "munbattan" with a two-dotted "t," meaning: scattered. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. The first view on "al-hab'a" is the best of the views.

The address in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you became﴾ is to all the world, because those described as companions of the left hand are not in the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Al-azwaj" means: types and kinds. Qatada said: these are the stations of people on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so the companions of the right hand﴾ begins a sentence, "ma" is a second beginning, and "companions of the right hand" is the predicate of "ma," and the whole clause is the predicate of the first beginning. In the speech there is a sense of magnification, as you say: "Zayd, what Zayd is!" and the like of this in the Qur'an is abundant. "Al-maymana" most evidently in its derivation is from the side of the right, and it has been said: from "yumn" (blessing). Likewise "al-mash'ama" may be from the left hand, or from "shu'm" (ill omen). This verse has been explained by both meanings, since the companions of the right hand are the fortunate ones concerning their own selves. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Rabi'. It seems that "yumn" and "shu'm" were derived from right and left, according to their custom regarding the auspicious and the inauspicious birds. Likewise "al-yumn" and "al-sham" were derived from the right and the left.

His saying, the Exalted: "and the foremost" begins a sentence, and the second "the foremost" — some grammarians said it is an adjective of the first. Sibawayh's view is that it is the predicate of the beginning, as you say: "the people, the people," and "you, you." This is for the sake of exalting and magnifying the matter, and the meaning is: "the foremost to faith, the foremost to the Garden and to mercy, those..." This meaning fits the beginning-and-predicate construction.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ is a beginning and predicate, and it stands in the position of the predicate according to the view of one who said the second "foremost" is an adjective. "Al-muqarrabun" means: near to God in the Garden of Eden. A group of people of knowledge said: this verse implies that the world on the Day of Resurrection is of three kinds: believers, who are on the right of the Throne, and there is the Garden; and disbelievers, who are on the left of the Throne, and there is the Fire. The discussion of the right and left of the Throne is similar to what was mentioned in Surat al-Kahf regarding right and left. It has been said about the companions of the right hand that they are those who take their book in their right hand, and about the companions of the left that they are those who take it in their left hand. According to this, the attribution of right and left is not to the Throne. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) said: the companions of the right are the children of believers. It has been said: the intended "right" and "left" of Adam (peace be upon him) are the two mentioned in the hadith of the Night Journey, in the black figures.

"The foremost" means: happiness had preceded for them, and their deeds in this world were a precedence to deeds of righteousness and to abandoning sins. This is a generality over all people, and the exegetes specified some of it. 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawda said: they are those who hasten to the mosques. Ibn Sirin said: they are those who prayed toward both qiblas. Ka'b said: they are the people of the Qur'an. It has been said: they are other than these, which are part of righteous deeds. It is narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the foremost, and he said: 'They are those who, when given the truth, accept it, and when asked for it, give it, and judge for people by the judgment they would give for themselves.'"

Talha ibn Musarrif read "fi jannati al-na'im" in the singular. "Al-muqarrabun" is an expression for the highest stations of humankind in the Hereafter. It has been said: [they are] reclining on woven thrones. It was said to 'Amir ibn 'Abd Qays on a day of a race: "Who won?" He said: "The ones brought near."

Commentary on Surat al-Waqi'a

It is Meccan by consensus among those whose opinion on the exegetes counts. It has been said that it contains verses that are Medinan, or that were revealed during a journey, but all of this is not established. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever persists in reciting Surat al-Waqi'a will never become poor." Also, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may God be pleased with him) invited Ibn Mas'ud (may God be pleased with him) to his stipend, but he refused to take it. He was told, "Take it for your dependents," and he said: "They recite Surat al-Waqi'a. I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever recites it will never become poor.'"

The author, Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him), said:

It contains mention of the Resurrection and of the portions of the self in the Hereafter, and understanding this is a wealth with no poverty in it. Whoever understands it occupies himself with preparation.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿When the Event occurs﴾ ﴿there is no denying its occurrence﴾ ﴿abasing and exalting﴾ ﴿when the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ ﴿and the mountains are crumbled into powder﴾ ﴿and become scattered dust﴾ ﴿and you become three kinds﴾ ﴿so the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ ﴿and the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand!﴾ ﴿and the foremost, the foremost﴾ ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Delight﴾.

"Al-Waqi'a" is one of the names of the Resurrection, like "al-Sakhkha," "al-Azifa," and "al-Tamma." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both). All of these are names that call for magnifying it and stressing the gravity of its matter. Al-Dahhak said: "al-Waqi'a" is the Blast, which is the blowing into the Trumpet. Some exegetes said: "al-Waqi'a" is the Rock of Jerusalem, which will fall at the Resurrection. All of these are meanings pertaining to the Resurrection.

"Kadhiba" may be a verbal noun, like "al-'Aqiba," "al-'Afiya," and "Khha'inat al-a'yun." The meaning would then be: there is no denial of it, nor any turning back. This is the view of Qatada and al-Hasan. It may also be an adjective for an implied noun, as if He, the Exalted, said: "there is no state of its occurrence that is false." Based on this, the expression may have two meanings: first, "kadhiba" means "that which is denied" regarding what He reported about it, and He called it "kadhiba" for this reason, as you say "a false story," meaning one in which lies are told. Second, "a false state," meaning its occurrence does not fail to happen, as you say: "So-and-so, when he charges, does not turn back."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿abasing and exalting﴾ is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: it is abasing and exalting. Al-Hasan, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, and Abu Haywa read "khafidatan rafi'atan" in the accusative, as a state following the state in "there is no denying its occurrence." You may follow the states as you may follow the predicates of a subject. The first reading is more well-known and more eloquent in meaning, because the position of a state in speech is that of something which, if it were not mentioned, one could do without, whereas the position of sentences that the predicate definitively confirms is the position of what matters.

People differed about the meaning of this abasing and exalting in this verse. Qatada and 'Uthman ibn 'Abdullah ibn Suraqa said: the Resurrection abases some peoples to the Fire and exalts other peoples to the Garden. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, and al-Dahhak said: the Blast lowers its voice so that the nearest hears it, and raises it so that the farthest hears it. Most of those who interpreted said: the Resurrection, through the splitting of the heaven, the earth and the mountains, and the collapse of this structure, raises some bodies and lowers others, so it is an expression for the intensity of the terror and turmoil.

The governing element of His saying, the Exalted: "when [it is] shaken" and "occurs" is "occurs," because this is a substitute for the first "when." Some have said that "occurs" is the governing element of the first, because the meaning of the conditional in both is strong, so it is like "whoever" and "whatever" in conditionals, which the verbs after them govern. It has also been said that "when" is annexed to "occurs," so it cannot govern it, and the governing element is an implied verb.

The meaning of "shaken" is: shaken and moved violently. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both). From it comes "the arrow shook in the target" when it trembles after landing. "Rajja" among people is a stirring matter. The lexicographers differed about the meaning of "bussat." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and 'Ikrima said its meaning is: crumbled to bits, as "al-basisa" is ground, which is parched flour, and it is said: "I moistened the flour" when I wet it with water and it remains crumbled. Al-Tabari cited in this:

"Do not bake a baking, nor crumble a crumbling"

This is the saying of a thief whom fear hurried away from the dough, so he said this to his two companions. Some lexicographers said: "bussat" means "was set in motion." They said: "al-khubz" is hard traveling and striking the earth with the hands, and "al-bass" is gentle traveling. They cited the verse:

"Do not bake a baking, nor set in motion a setting in motion, and flank for us Nahshal and 'Abs"

Abu 'Uthman al-Lughawi mentioned this in the book "al-Af'al."

"Al-hab'a" is the fine particles that fly in the air and are hardly seen except in sunlight when it enters through a window. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Qatada said: "al-hab'a" is what flies off from the dryness of plants. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) said: "al-hab'a" is what flies off from the hooves of horses and beasts. Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) also said: "al-hab'a" is what flies off from sparks of fire, and when it is extinguished nothing is found. "Al-munbath" with a three-dotted "th" means: spread throughout all the air. Al-Nakha'i read "munbattan" with a two-dotted "t," meaning: scattered. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. The first view on "al-hab'a" is the best of the views.

The address in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and you became﴾ is to all the world, because those described as companions of the left hand are not in the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). "Al-azwaj" means: types and kinds. Qatada said: these are the stations of people on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so the companions of the right hand﴾ begins a sentence, "ma" is a second beginning, and "companions of the right hand" is the predicate of "ma," and the whole clause is the predicate of the first beginning. In the speech there is a sense of magnification, as you say: "Zayd, what Zayd is!" and the like of this in the Qur'an is abundant. "Al-maymana" most evidently in its derivation is from the side of the right, and it has been said: from "yumn" (blessing). Likewise "al-mash'ama" may be from the left hand, or from "shu'm" (ill omen). This verse has been explained by both meanings, since the companions of the right hand are the fortunate ones concerning their own selves. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Rabi'. It seems that "yumn" and "shu'm" were derived from right and left, according to their custom regarding the auspicious and the inauspicious birds. Likewise "al-yumn" and "al-sham" were derived from the right and the left.

His saying, the Exalted: "and the foremost" begins a sentence, and the second "the foremost" — some grammarians said it is an adjective of the first. Sibawayh's view is that it is the predicate of the beginning, as you say: "the people, the people," and "you, you." This is for the sake of exalting and magnifying the matter, and the meaning is: "the foremost to faith, the foremost to the Garden and to mercy, those..." This meaning fits the beginning-and-predicate construction.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿those are the ones brought near﴾ is a beginning and predicate, and it stands in the position of the predicate according to the view of one who said the second "foremost" is an adjective. "Al-muqarrabun" means: near to God in the Garden of Eden. A group of people of knowledge said: this verse implies that the world on the Day of Resurrection is of three kinds: believers, who are on the right of the Throne, and there is the Garden; and disbelievers, who are on the left of the Throne, and there is the Fire. The discussion of the right and left of the Throne is similar to what was mentioned in Surat al-Kahf regarding right and left. It has been said about the companions of the right hand that they are those who take their book in their right hand, and about the companions of the left that they are those who take it in their left hand. According to this, the attribution of right and left is not to the Throne. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him) said: the companions of the right are the children of believers. It has been said: the intended "right" and "left" of Adam (peace be upon him) are the two mentioned in the hadith of the Night Journey, in the black figures.

"The foremost" means: happiness had preceded for them, and their deeds in this world were a precedence to deeds of righteousness and to abandoning sins. This is a generality over all people, and the exegetes specified some of it. 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawda said: they are those who hasten to the mosques. Ibn Sirin said: they are those who prayed toward both qiblas. Ka'b said: they are the people of the Qur'an. It has been said: they are other than these, which are part of righteous deeds. It is narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the foremost, and he said: 'They are those who, when given the truth, accept it, and when asked for it, give it, and judge for people by the judgment they would give for themselves.'"

Talha ibn Musarrif read "fi jannati al-na'im" in the singular. "Al-muqarrabun" is an expression for the highest stations of humankind in the Hereafter. It has been said: [they are] reclining on woven thrones. It was said to 'Amir ibn 'Abd Qays on a day of a race: "Who won?" He said: "The ones brought near."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 56, verse 13–26:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿A multitude of the earlier generations﴾ ﴿and a few of the later generations.﴾ ﴿On thrones woven with gold and precious stones,﴾ ﴿reclining upon them, facing one another.﴾ ﴿There will circulate among them youths of everlasting youth,﴾ ﴿with goblets, ewers, and a cup from a flowing spring,﴾ ﴿they will not be affected with headache thereby, nor will they be intoxicated;﴾ ﴿and fruit of whatever they choose,﴾ ﴿and the flesh of fowl of whatever they desire.﴾ ﴿And theirs will be wide-eyed maidens,﴾ ﴿like pearls well-guarded,﴾ ﴿as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿They will hear therein no vain talk, nor any sinful speech,﴾ ﴿only the saying: "Peace, peace."﴾

"Al-thulla" (a multitude): a group and a company. It is used for both few and many. The wording in this usage indicates that the group of the earlier generations is greater than the group of the later generations, which is what is expressed by "few." The interpreters differed on the meaning of this. Some said — its statement was related by Makki — that what is meant by this are the prophets, peace be upon them, because they were greater in number at the beginning of the world. Al-Hasan and others said: what is meant are the foremost of the earlier nations and the foremost of this Ummah. This is either that the companions of the prophets, peace be upon them, together with their multitudes, are compared to the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, and those are greater in number without doubt; or that the companions of the prophets, peace be upon them, from among those who preceded in the midst of the earlier nations are compared to the foremost of this entire Ummah, and those are greater. It is related that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, grieved over the fewness of the foremost of this Ummah according to this interpretation, so there was revealed: ﴿A multitude of the earlier generations﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 39] ﴿and a multitude of the later generations﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 40], and they were content. It is related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she interpreted that the two groups within the Ummah of every prophet are: at the beginning, a multitude, and at the end of the Ummah, a few. The Prophet ﷺ said, as is related from him: "The two groups are in my Ummah: the foremost of the beginning of the Ummah is a multitude, and the foremost of its remainder until the Day of Resurrection is a few."

Al-Jumhur read "surur" with a dammah on the ra'. Abu al-Samal read "suraru" with a fatha on the ra'. "Al-mawdunah" means that which is woven, with some of its parts arranged upon others like the rings of a coat of mail, for a coat of mail is mawdunah. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And of the weaving of Dawud is a mawdunah, moving with the tribe, caravan after caravan."

Likewise a basket of palm fronds and the like is mawdunah. From this is the "wadin" of the camel, which is its girth, because it is mawdun (woven). It is like qatil and jarih. From this is his saying:

"Toward you she hastens, restless, her girth, with her unborn young lying across her belly,
differing from the religion of the Christians is her religion."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: these "surur mawdunah" are interlaced with gold. 'Ikrimah said: they are latticed with pearls and rubies. "Muttaki'in" and "mutaqabilin" are circumstantial clauses (hal), and in them is a pronoun in the nominative. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "muttaki'in 'alayha nai'mIn" (reclining upon them, at ease).

"Al-wildan": young attendants. It is an expression meaning that they are young in age. He described them with "everlasting" (khuld), although everything in Paradise is like that, as an indication that they remain in the state of youth, never growing old. Mujahid said: they do not die. Al-Farra' said: "mukhalladun" means "adorned with earrings of khaladat," which is a type of earring. The first (meaning) is more correct, because the Arabs say of one who has grown but has not gone grey: "innahu lamukhallad" (he is indeed everlasting-young).

"Al-akwab": vessels for drinking that have neither handle nor spout. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: they are jugs of silver. Abu Salih said: their mouths are round. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: they have no handles. "Al-ibriq": that which has a spout. Mujahid said: and a handle. It is among the vessels of wine for the Arabs. From this is the saying of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"They called one another to the morning drink, and there stood up a slave-girl with an ewer in her right hand."

"Al-ka's": the vessel prepared for drinking with it, on condition that it contains wine or nabidh, or something of that sort. When it is empty, it is still attributed to its kind, whether glass or otherwise, and a vessel containing water or milk is not called ka's.

His saying, Exalted is He: "min ma'in" — Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: its meaning is: from flowing wine. Its form is maf'ul; its origin is ma'yun. This is also the interpretation of Qatadah. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they will not be affected with headache thereby﴾ — most of the exegetes went to the view that the meaning is: the headache that befalls the heads from the wine of this world will not reach them. Others said: its meaning is: they will not be separated from it, in the sense that their pleasure will not be cut off by any cause, as the people of worldly wine are separated by various kinds of separation. This is like His saying: "The clouds part away from Madinah..." — the hadith.

His saying, Exalted is He: "wa la yunzifun" — Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: its meaning is: their intellects will not depart through intoxication. "Al-nazif" is the one who is intoxicated. From this is the saying of the poet:

"............ he drank the nazif with the cold water of al-Hashraj."

Ibn Abi Ishaq read "wa la yanzifun" with a kasra on the za' and a fatha on the ya', from "nazafa al-bi'r" when he drew out its water; so its meaning is: their wine is complete and exhausted. Thus said Abu al-Fath. Abu Hatim related it from Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and 'Isa, with a dammah on the ya' and a kasra on the za'. He said: its meaning is: their drink does not run out. The Arabs say: "anzafa al-rajulu 'abratahu" (the man exhausted his tear). They also say "anzafa" when one becomes intoxicated. From this is the saying of al-Ubayrid:

"By my life, if you have become intoxicated or sobered, you are a wretched company of drinkers, O family of Abjar."

He conjoined "al-fakihah" (fruit) to "al-ka's wa al-abariq" (cups and ewers).

His saying, Exalted is He: "mimma yashtahun" — it is related concerning it that the servant sees a bird flying, desires it, and it descends to him as he desired; and perhaps he eats from it varieties according to the variation of his desire, along with much else related on this meaning.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "wa hurin 'in" with a kasra (in the genitive). This is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-A'mash, Abu al-Qa'qa' and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud read "wa huran 'inan" with a fatha (accusative). The rest of the seven read "wa hurun 'inun" with a damma (nominative). All these readings are grammatically governed according to the meaning and not the wording. The genitive reading: it is as if the meaning is, "It is said: you are made to enjoy all this and wide-eyed maidens." The accusative reading: it is as if the meaning is, "And you are given all this and wide-eyed maidens." The nominative reading: it is as if the meaning is, "For them is all this, and wide-eyed maidens." It is permissible that "wa hurun" be conjoined to the pronoun resting in "muttaki'in." Abu 'Ali said: it was not emphasized, because the length of the speech serves as a substitute for emphasis. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to "al-wildan," though the circulation of the maidens would be disturbing. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to the implied pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: "on thrones." In all of this there is consideration. The meaning of "hurun 'inun" has already been mentioned. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "wa hirin 'in."

Glorified is He, specified the hidden pearl because its color is purest and furthest from any admixture. Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about this comparison, and he said: "Their clarity is like the clarity of a pearl in its shell, which no hand has touched." His saying "as a reward for what they used to do," that is: these ranks and blessings are according to their deeds, for it is related that the dwellings and the shares in Paradise are apportioned according to the measure of deeds. Yet entry into Paradise itself is by the mercy and bounty of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, not by the deed of any doer. As for this bounty, and that entry into it is not by the deed of any doer, there is a sahih hadith: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Nor I, unless Allah covers me with a bounty and mercy from Him."

"Al-laghw": idle talk, of obscenity or otherwise. "Al-ta'thim" is a verbal noun, meaning that no one there is made sinful by another's speech, nor by his own speech, such as one who hears something and is pained by hearing it. "Qilan" is an exception, and the exception is connected (muttasil). Some said it is disconnected (munqati'). "Salaman" is an adjective of "qil," as if He, Exalted is He, said: "except a word free of these faults and others." Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj also said: "salaman" is a verbal noun whose governing word is "qilan," as if He, Exalted is He, mentioned that they say to one another: "Salaman, salaman." Some grammarians said: "salaman" is in the accusative governed by an implied verb whose estimate is: "They were made to submit, submission."

The interpreters differed on the meaning of this. Some said — its statement was related by Makki — that what is meant by this are the prophets, peace be upon them, because they were greater in number at the beginning of the world. Al-Hasan and others said: what is meant are the foremost of the earlier nations and the foremost of this Ummah. This is either that the companions of the prophets, peace be upon them, together with their multitudes, are compared to the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, and those are greater in number without doubt; or that the companions of the prophets, peace be upon them, from among those who preceded in the midst of the earlier nations are compared to the foremost of this entire Ummah, and those are greater. It is related that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, grieved over the fewness of the foremost of this Ummah according to this interpretation, so there was revealed: ﴿A multitude of the earlier generations﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 39] ﴿and a multitude of the later generations﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 40], and they were content. It is related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she interpreted that the two groups within the Ummah of every prophet are: at the beginning, a multitude, and at the end of the Ummah, a few. The Prophet ﷺ said, as is related from him: "The two groups are in my Ummah: the foremost of the beginning of the Ummah is a multitude, and the foremost of its remainder until the Day of Resurrection is a few."

Al-Jumhur read "surur" with a dammah on the ra'. Abu al-Samal read "suraru" with a fatha on the ra'. "Al-mawdunah" means that which is woven, with some of its parts arranged upon others like the rings of a coat of mail, for a coat of mail is mawdunah. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And of the weaving of Dawud is a mawdunah, moving with the tribe, caravan after caravan."

Likewise a basket of palm fronds and the like is mawdunah. From this is the "wadin" of the camel, which is its girth, because it is mawdun (woven). It is like qatil and jarih. From this is his saying:

"Toward you she hastens, restless, her girth, with her unborn young lying across her belly,
differing from the religion of the Christians is her religion."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: these "surur mawdunah" are interlaced with gold. 'Ikrimah said: they are latticed with pearls and rubies. "Muttaki'in" and "mutaqabilin" are circumstantial clauses (hal), and in them is a pronoun in the nominative. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "muttaki'in 'alayha nai'mIn" (reclining upon them, at ease).

"Al-wildan": young attendants. It is an expression meaning that they are young in age. He described them with "everlasting" (khuld), although everything in Paradise is like that, as an indication that they remain in the state of youth, never growing old. Mujahid said: they do not die. Al-Farra' said: "mukhalladun" means "adorned with earrings of khaladat," which is a type of earring. The first (meaning) is more correct, because the Arabs say of one who has grown but has not gone grey: "innahu lamukhallad" (he is indeed everlasting-young).

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: they have no handles. "Al-ibriq": that which has a spout. Mujahid said: and a handle. It is among the vessels of wine for the Arabs. From this is the saying of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"They called one another to the morning drink, and there stood up a slave-girl with an ewer in her right hand."

"Al-ka's": the vessel prepared for drinking with it, on condition that it contains wine or nabidh, or something of that sort. When it is empty, it is still attributed to its kind, whether glass or otherwise, and a vessel containing water or milk is not called ka's.

His saying, Exalted is He: "min ma'in" — Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: its meaning is: from flowing wine. Its form is maf'ul; its origin is ma'yun. This is also the interpretation of Qatadah. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿they will not be affected with headache thereby﴾ — most of the exegetes went to the view that the meaning is: the headache that befalls the heads from the wine of this world will not reach them. Others said: its meaning is: they will not be separated from it, in the sense that their pleasure will not be cut off by any cause, as the people of worldly wine are separated by various kinds of separation. This is like His saying: "The clouds part away from Madinah..." — the hadith.

His saying, Exalted is He: "wa la yunzifun" — Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: its meaning is: their intellects will not depart through intoxication. "Al-nazif" is the one who is intoxicated. From this is the saying of the poet:

"............ he drank the nazif with the cold water of al-Hashraj."

Thus said Abu al-Fath. Abu Hatim related it from Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Jahdari, al-A'mash, Talhah, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and 'Isa, with a dammah on the ya' and a kasra on the za'. He said: its meaning is: their drink does not run out. The Arabs say: "anzafa al-rajulu 'abratahu" (the man exhausted his tear). They also say "anzafa" when one becomes intoxicated. From this is the saying of al-Ubayrid:

"By my life, if you have become intoxicated or sobered, you are a wretched company of drinkers, O family of Abjar."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 56, verse 27–40:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ ﴿And acacias with layered fruit﴾ ﴿And extended shade﴾ ﴿And water poured out﴾ ﴿And fruit in abundance﴾ ﴿Neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ ﴿And raised couches﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special creation﴾ ﴿And made them virgins﴾ ﴿Loving, of equal age﴾ ﴿For the companions of the right hand﴾ ﴿A multitude from the former peoples﴾ ﴿And a multitude from the latter peoples﴾

"Al-sidr" (lote-tree) is a well-known tree, the one that is called the tree of Umm Ghaylan. It is of the 'idah (thorny trees) and has thorns. In Paradise there is a tree in its (real) form, whose fruit is like the jars of Hajar, good in taste and fragrance. He, exalted is He, described it as "makhdud" (without thorns), meaning its thorns are cut off, so there is no harm in it. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

؎ Indeed the gardens in the Gardens are shaded, in them are maidens, and their lote-trees are without thorns.

Some exegetes interpreted "makhdud" as "laden with its fruit (heavy with its load)." Others said it means the cutting off of thorns, and this is the correct view. As for its being laden, that is its bounty. It is narrated from al-Dahhak that some of the Companions admired the lote-trees of Ta'if and said, "Would that we had the like of this in the Hereafter," and then this verse was revealed. For those who examine the matter closely, there is here an indication that this cutting of thorns corresponds to their deeds by which they were safe, for the people of the right hand are penitents for whom there is peace, and they are not foremost (in rank).

"Al-talh" likewise is among the 'idah, a large tree with many thorns, and in Paradise it is likened to it in many attributes that are contrary to the state of this world. "Mandud" means: its fruit is arranged one upon another from its base up to its top. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others, recited "wa-talhin mandud" (with banana-bunches). It was said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is only 'wa-talh'." He said: "What has the talh to do with Paradise?" It was said to him: "Shall we correct it in the Mushaf?" He said: "Indeed, the Mushaf today is not to be stirred or changed." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "Al-talh" is the banana, and Mujahid and 'Ata' said the same. Al-Hasan said: "It is not the banana, but a tree whose shade is cool and pleasant."

"Extended shade" means that which the sun does not dispel. This is explained by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider on a swift horse would travel a hundred years without crossing it. Recite, if you wish: 'And extended shade.'" And there are other hadiths to this effect. Mujahid said: this shade is from its talh and its sidr.

His saying, the Exalted: "And water poured out," meaning: without the season passing as with the fruits of this world. "Nor forbidden," meaning: by distance of reaching, nor by thorns that harm in its trees, nor by any of the aspects by which the fruits of this world are withheld.

The majority of readers recited "wa-furushin" with a damma on the ra'. Abu Haywa recited "wa-furshun" with sukun on it. Al-furush are the beds, and it is narrated through Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the height of the bed in it is five hundred years. This, and Allah knows best, is not authentic; and if it is accepted, it is an interpretation departing from its apparent meaning. Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: by "furush" is meant the women. "Marfu'ah" means in ranks and stations, and from this meaning is the saying of the poet:

؎ You sat spreading out the cloth, insulting me in the presence of the Messenger, but you were neither truthful nor right.

And from this is the saying of another, in enumerating his favours to his in-law: "And I spread for you my noble (daughter)."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special creation﴾. Qatadah said: the pronoun refers to the "Hur al-'In" mentioned before. This is distant, because that narrative has concluded as a whole. Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar said: He mentioned them in His saying, "And raised couches," so for this reason He returned the pronoun though no mention preceded, since the meaning indicates the intended referent. This is like His saying: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32] and similar. "Anshaanahunna" means: We created them one thing after another. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said in explanation of this verse: "Your old women in this world are blear-eyed and rheumy-eyed." He, upon him be prayer and peace, also said to an old woman: "Indeed Paradise is not entered by an old woman," so she grieved, and he said: "Indeed when you enter Paradise you will be created a different creation."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And made them virgins﴾. It was said: its meaning is those who are constantly virgins; whenever the one who has intercourse returns to her, he finds her a virgin. "'Uruban" is the plural of "'arub," who is the one who shows affection to her husband by displaying her love for him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also described them as "al-'awashiq" (the ardent lovers). From this is the saying of Labid:

؎ And in the litters are 'urub (loving women), not of indecent conduct, whose hips are full, and the eye is dazzled before them.

Ibn Zayd said: "'Uruban" means those good in speech. The word 'urub may also come as an attribute of blame with a meaning other than this, namely those corrupt in character, as if they had been made 'arab (Arabized, i.e., non-Arab in manner). From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ And there is no substitute for the mother of 'Uthman, a wide-hipped, black woman, with a wilful bridle, a stubborn one.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i recited "'urudan" with a damma on the ra'. Hamzah, al-Hasan and al-A'mash recited "'urban" with sukun on it, and this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. There was variance from Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim.

His saying, the Exalted: "Atraban" means: in form and stature, such that the beholder says: they are of one age. The "tirb" is the one who touched the dust together with his tirb (peer) at one time. Qatadah said: "Atraban" means: of one age. It is narrated that the people of Paradise are about the age of a fourteen-year-old in youth and freshness; and it was said: like the sons of thirty-three years, beardless, white, with kohl-darkened eyes.

People differed concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A multitude from the former peoples﴾ ﴿And a multitude from the latter peoples﴾. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others said: The former are the earlier nations, among whom is a great company who are the companions of the right hand; and the latter are this Ummah, among whom is a great company who are the people of the right hand.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Rather, all of them, except those who were among the foremost.

Some of the interpreters said: These two groups are within the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The two-thirds are from my Ummah." Accordingly, the Followers who do good and whoever follows their course form the first multitude, and the rest of the Ummah form the other multitude at the end of time.

Qatadah said: "Atraban" means: of one age. It is narrated that the people of Paradise are about the age of a fourteen-year-old in youth and freshness; and it was said: like the sons of thirty-three years, beardless, white, with kohl-darkened eyes.

People differed concerning His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A multitude from the former peoples﴾ ﴿And a multitude from the latter peoples﴾. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others said: The former are the earlier nations, among whom is a great company who are the companions of the right hand; and the latter are this Ummah, among whom is a great company who are the people of the right hand.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Rather, all of them, except those who were among the foremost.

Some of the interpreters said: These two groups are within the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The two-thirds are from my Ummah." Accordingly, the Followers who do good and whoever follows their course form the first multitude, and the rest of the Ummah form the other multitude at the end of time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 56, verse 27–40:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand?﴾ ﴿Among lote-trees without thorns﴾ ﴿And acacias with layered fruit﴾ ﴿And extended shade﴾ ﴿And water poured out﴾ ﴿And fruit in abundance﴾ ﴿Neither cut off nor forbidden﴾ ﴿And raised couches﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special creation﴾ ﴿And made them virgins﴾ ﴿Loving, of equal age﴾ ﴿For the companions of the right hand﴾ ﴿A multitude from the former peoples﴾ ﴿And a multitude from the latter peoples﴾

"Al-sidr" (lote-tree) is a well-known tree, the one that is called the tree of Umm Ghaylan. It is of the 'idah (thorny trees) and has thorns. In Paradise there is a tree in its (real) form, whose fruit is like the jars of Hajar, good in taste and fragrance. He, exalted is He, described it as "makhdud" (without thorns), meaning its thorns are cut off, so there is no harm in it. Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

؎ Indeed the gardens in the Gardens are shaded, in them are maidens, and their lote-trees are without thorns.

Some exegetes interpreted "makhdud" as "laden with its fruit (heavy with its load)." Others said it means the cutting off of thorns, and this is the correct view. As for its being laden, that is its bounty. It is narrated from al-Dahhak that some of the Companions admired the lote-trees of Ta'if and said, "Would that we had the like of this in the Hereafter," and then this verse was revealed. For those who examine the matter closely, there is here an indication that this cutting of thorns corresponds to their deeds by which they were safe, for the people of the right hand are penitents for whom there is peace, and they are not foremost (in rank).

"Al-talh" likewise is among the 'idah, a large tree with many thorns, and in Paradise it is likened to it in many attributes that are contrary to the state of this world. "Mandud" means: its fruit is arranged one upon another from its base up to its top. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others, recited "wa-talhin mandud" (with banana-bunches). It was said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is only 'wa-talh'." He said: "What has the talh to do with Paradise?" It was said to him: "Shall we correct it in the Mushaf?" He said: "Indeed, the Mushaf today is not to be stirred or changed." 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, said: "Al-talh" is the banana, and Mujahid and 'Ata' said the same. Al-Hasan said: "It is not the banana, but a tree whose shade is cool and pleasant."

"Extended shade" means that which the sun does not dispel. This is explained by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider on a swift horse would travel a hundred years without crossing it. Recite, if you wish: 'And extended shade.'" And there are other hadiths to this effect. Mujahid said: this shade is from its talh and its sidr.

His saying, the Exalted: "And water poured out," meaning: without the season passing as with the fruits of this world. "Nor forbidden," meaning: by distance of reaching, nor by thorns that harm in its trees, nor by any of the aspects by which the fruits of this world are withheld.

The majority of readers recited "wa-furushin" with a damma on the ra'. Abu Haywa recited "wa-furshun" with sukun on it. Al-furush are the beds, and it is narrated through Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, that the height of the bed in it is five hundred years. This, and Allah knows best, is not authentic; and if it is accepted, it is an interpretation departing from its apparent meaning. Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: by "furush" is meant the women. "Marfu'ah" means in ranks and stations, and from this meaning is the saying of the poet:

؎ You sat spreading out the cloth, insulting me in the presence of the Messenger, but you were neither truthful nor right.

And from this is the saying of another, in enumerating his favours to his in-law: "And I spread for you my noble (daughter)."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a special creation﴾. Qatadah said: the pronoun refers to the "Hur al-'In" mentioned before. This is distant, because that narrative has concluded as a whole. Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar said: He mentioned them in His saying, "And raised couches," so for this reason He returned the pronoun though no mention preceded, since the meaning indicates the intended referent. This is like His saying: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32] and similar. "Anshaanahunna" means: We created them one thing after another. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said in explanation of this verse: "Your old women in this world are blear-eyed and rheumy-eyed." He, upon him be prayer and peace, also said to an old woman: "Indeed Paradise is not entered by an old woman," so she grieved, and he said: "Indeed when you enter Paradise you will be created a different creation."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And made them virgins﴾. It was said: its meaning is those who are constantly virgins; whenever the one who has intercourse returns to her, he finds her a virgin. "'Uruban" is the plural of "'arub," who is the one who shows affection to her husband by displaying her love for him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also described them as "al-'awashiq" (the ardent lovers). From this is the saying of Labid:

؎ And in the litters are 'urub (loving women), not of indecent conduct, whose hips are full, and the eye is dazzled before them.

Ibn Zayd said: "'Uruban" means those good in speech. The word 'urub may also come as an attribute of blame with a meaning other than this, namely those corrupt in character, as if they had been made 'arab (Arabized, i.e., non-Arab in manner). From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ And there is no substitute for the mother of 'Uthman, a wide-hipped, black woman, with a wilful bridle, a stubborn one.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 56, verse 41–50:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And the companions of the left hand — what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ ﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾ ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾ ﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent (mutrafin)﴾ ﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾ ﴿And they used to say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers, the earlier ones?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, the former and the latter﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day."﴾

I'rab of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the companions of the left hand — what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ It has already been discussed in its counterpart, and in this speech there is the meaning of disparagement of them and magnification of their calamity.

And "al-samum" (scorching wind): the most intense of dry heat with no moisture in it.

And "al-hamim" (boiling water): the black one, and it is an intensive form. People differed concerning this black thing that shades the people of the Fire, what is it? Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Malik, and Ibn Zayd said: it is the smoke, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: it is the enclosure (suradiq) of the Fire that encircles its people, for it rises from every direction until it shades them. Al-Naqqash related that "al-yahmum" is one of the names of Jahannam, and Ibn Kaysan said it, and Ibn Buraydah and Ibn Zayd also said, in the book of al-Tha'labi: it is a black mountain in the Fire to whose peak the people of the Fire flee for refuge, and they find it the most severe and bitterest of things.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant.﴾ Al-Tabari and others said: its meaning is that it has no attribute of praise in shade, and this is like when you say: "a garment that is pleasant (karim)" and "a lineage that is noble," meaning by that that it has attributes of praise. It may also be understood as describing it as lacking nobility, in the sense that there is no honour for them. This is because a person in this world may endure a bad place for the sake of an honour he receives there from someone; so this shade in the Fire combines being of bad quality with them being humiliated in it.

(p-202) And "al-mutraf": the one made luxurious in excess and immersion (in pleasures). And "yusirrun" means: they hold a belief from which they do not intend to desist. Ibn Zayd said: they do not repent nor seek forgiveness. And "al-hinth": sin. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever has three children die who have not reached the hinth..." (the hadith), by which he, peace and blessings be upon him, meant: who have not reached puberty, so that sins are not attached to them. Al-Khattabi said: in the speech of the Arabs, "al-hinth" is a heavy burden, and sin is likened to it. The commentators differed about what is meant by this sin. Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd said: it is shirk, and this is the apparent meaning. Others said, as Makki mentioned: it is the violation of their oath, which is contained in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], in denying the resurrection; and this also includes disbelief, so holding it in its general sense is more appropriate. Al-Sha'bi said: "al-hinth al-'azim" is the perjurous oath (al-yamin al-ghamus).

The difference of the readers concerning His saying, the Exalted, "a-idha" and "a-inna" has already been mentioned. What is specific to this place is that Ibn 'Amir departs here from his usual practice and reads "ayidha" and "ayinna" with both hamzas made clear, as an interrogative. Abu Bakr narrated it from 'Asim in His saying, the Exalted: "a-inna lamab'uthun." The governing element in His saying, the Exalted, "a-idha" is a hidden verb indicated by His saying, the Exalted: "lamab'uthun," its estimate being: "Will we be raised, or gathered?" What follows it does not govern it, because it is in the genitive by annexation. Isa al-Thaqafi read "mutna" with a damma on the mim, while the majority of people read "mitna" with a kasra on it, and this is according to the dialect of one who says "mitta amutu," on the pattern of "fa'ila yaf'alu" with the 'ayn kasra and the present with damma; and from the Arabs there is not related from this pattern except this word and another, which is "fadala yafdulu." Some readers read "aw abaa'una" with the waw of "aw" sukun, and the meaning of the verse is the denial that they and their fathers would be raised on one and the same degree of improbability. The majority read "awa-aba'una" with the waw vowelled, as a conjunctive waw into which the interrogative alif has entered, and its meaning is the intensity of denial concerning the fathers (p-203), as though they denied that they would be raised, then brought up a mention of the resurrection of the fathers as even more remote. This is clear to the people of knowledge of the Arabic tongue.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to inform them that the whole creation will be gathered and raised for a known, appointed day. "Miqat" is a form of "waqt" (time), like "mi'ad" from "wa'd" (promise).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 56, verse 41–50:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And the companions of the left hand — what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾ ﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾ ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾ ﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent (mutrafin)﴾ ﴿And they used to persist in the great violation﴾ ﴿And they used to say, "When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected? And our forefathers, the earlier ones?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, the former and the latter﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day."﴾

I'rab of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the companions of the left hand — what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ It has already been discussed in its counterpart, and in this speech there is the meaning of disparagement of them and magnification of their calamity.

And "al-samum" (scorching wind): the most intense of dry heat with no moisture in it.

And "al-hamim" (boiling water): the black one, and it is an intensive form. People differed concerning this black thing that shades the people of the Fire, what is it? Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Malik, and Ibn Zayd said: it is the smoke, and this is the view of the majority. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: it is the enclosure (suradiq) of the Fire that encircles its people, for it rises from every direction until it shades them. Al-Naqqash related that "al-yahmum" is one of the names of Jahannam, and Ibn Kaysan said it, and Ibn Buraydah and Ibn Zayd also said, in the book of al-Tha'labi: it is a black mountain in the Fire to whose peak the people of the Fire flee for refuge, and they find it the most severe and bitterest of things.

It may also be understood as describing it as lacking nobility, in the sense that there is no honour for them. This is because a person in this world may endure a bad place for the sake of an honour he receives there from someone; so this shade in the Fire combines being of bad quality with them being humiliated in it.

(p-202) And "al-mutraf": the one made luxurious in excess and immersion (in pleasures). And "yusirrun" means: they hold a belief from which they do not intend to desist. Ibn Zayd said: they do not repent nor seek forgiveness. And "al-hinth": sin. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever has three children die who have not reached the hinth..." (the hadith), by which he, peace and blessings be upon him, meant: who have not reached puberty, so that sins are not attached to them. Al-Khattabi said: in the speech of the Arabs, "al-hinth" is a heavy burden, and sin is likened to it. The commentators differed about what is meant by this sin. Others said, as Makki mentioned: it is the violation of their oath, which is contained in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], in denying the resurrection; and this also includes disbelief, so holding it in its general sense is more appropriate. Al-Sha'bi said: "al-hinth al-'azim" is the perjurous oath (al-yamin al-ghamus).

Abu Bakr narrated it from 'Asim in His saying, the Exalted: "a-inna lamab'uthun." This is clear to the people of knowledge of the Arabic tongue.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to inform them that the whole creation will be gathered and raised for a known, appointed day. "Miqat" is a form of "waqt" (time), like "mi'ad" from "wa'd" (promise).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 56, verse 51–62:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Then indeed you, O you who are astray and deniers,﴾ ﴿will be eating from a tree of zaqqum,﴾ ﴿filling your bellies with it,﴾ ﴿and drinking on top of it from the boiling water,﴾ ﴿drinking as thirsty camels drink.﴾ ﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Recompense.﴾ ﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ ﴿Have you considered the semen you emit?﴾ ﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ ﴿We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone﴾ ﴿in replacing your likenesses and producing you in what you do not know.﴾ ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so why do you not remember?﴾

His, the Exalted's, saying: "Then indeed you" is an address to the disbelievers of Quraysh and whoever is in their condition. The "min" in His saying "from a tree" may be partitive (lil-tab'id) and may be for the beginning of the extent (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). The "min" in His saying "from zaqqum" is for explaining the genus (li-bayan al-jins). The pronoun in "from it" refers to the tree, and the "min" is partitive or for the beginning of the extent. The pronoun in "on it" refers to what is eaten or to the eating. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "la-akilina min shajaratin" in the singular.

As for "al-Him" (the thirsty camels), Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: it is the plural of "ahyam," which is the camel afflicted with al-Hiyam (with a damma on the ha'), a thirst-causing disease, with which the camel keeps drinking until it dies or becomes severely sickened. The female is "haya'." Some said: it is the plural of "hay'a," like "a'yana" and "'ayn" and "bayda'" and "bid." Other people said: it is the plural of "hA'im" and "ha'ima," and this also comes from this same meaning, because when a camel is afflicted with that, it wanders off on its face and goes away. Ibn 'Abbas and Sufyan al-Thawri said: al-Him here means the sands that are not satisfied with water, because al-Hiyam (with a fatha on the ha') is the crumbling, heaped, piled-up sand. Tha'lab said: al-Hiyam (with a damma on the ha') is the sand that does not hold together. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "shariba al-Him" with a fatha on the shin, and this is the reading of al-A'raj, Ibn al-Musayyab, Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab, Malik ibn Dinar and Ibn Jurayj, and there is no disagreement that it is a verbal noun (masdar). Mujahid read "shirbu al-Him" with a kasra on the shin, and there is no disagreement that it is a noun (ism). The people of Madina and the rest of the seven read "shurba al-Him" with a damma on the shin, and there is disagreement about it: some said it is a verbal noun, and others said it is a noun for what is drunk.

"Nuzul" is the first thing a guest eats. 'Amr, in the narration of Ibn 'Ayyash, read "nuzuluhum" with a sukun on the zay, and the rest, and al-Yazidi from Abu 'Amr, read it with a damma on the zay; both have the same meaning, like "al-shughl" and "al-shughul." "Al-Din" means the recompense.

Then the Exalted informed that He is the Creator, and urged belief in a rebuking manner. Then the Exalted presented the argument that inspires belief. A disbeliever objected and said: "Why should I believe?" So it was said to him: "Have you considered such-and-such?" and so on, the verses. There is no created being who is unaware that the semen that comes out of him has no action, will, or power of his own in it. The "am" in His saying "Or are We the Creators?" is not the equalizing conjunction (al-mu'adalah) according to Sibawayh, because the verb has been repeated; the equalizing "am" for him is in "Did Zayd stand, or 'Amr?" The one in this verse is an equalizing "am" according to some grammarians. When the two verbs differ, it is by consensus not an equalizing "am." The majority read "tumnun" with a damma on the ta', and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Abu al-Samal read "tamnun" with a fatha on the ta'. It is said: "amna al-rajul" and "manna al-rajul" have one meaning.

The majority of reciters read "nahnu qaddarna" with a shadda on the dal, and Kuthayyir alone read "nahnu qadarna" with the dal lightened. The meaning in both may be: We decreed and established; and it may mean: We made equal and ordered the earlier and later, that is, We made death into ranks, so the world does not die all at once, but in an order that no one escapes. Al-Tabari said: the meaning of the verse is: We decreed death among you on the condition that We replace your likenesses, that is, a group dies and We replace it with another group, generation after generation. His, the Exalted's, saying: "and We are not to be outdone" in replacing you, if We wish it, and in producing you in attributes that your deeds do not reach and your thoughts do not encompass. Al-Hasan said: [this refers to] your being transformed into apes and swine.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Hasan interpreted this because the verse tends toward warning, and the word "sabq" here comes in the manner of His, may blessings and peace be upon him, saying: "If you are able not to be overcome in the prayer before the rising of the sun and the prayer before its setting, then do so; do not let them escape you."

The majority of people read "al-nash'ah" with a sukun on the shin. Qatadah, Abu al-Ashhab, and Abu 'Amr in one report read "al-nash'ah" with a fatha and with the long vowel. Most exegetes said: it points to the creation of Adam and stopped on it, because you will not find anyone who denies that he is from the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, and that he is from clay. Some said: by "the first creation" he meant the creation of a human in childhood, so a person knows his own creation by what he sees of the creation of others.

Then the Exalted urged remembrance and reflection that leads to faith. The majority read "fa-lawla tadhakkarun" with a shadda on the dhal, and Talha read "fa-lawla tadhkurun" with a sukun on the dhal and a damma on the kaf. This verse is a clear text for the use of analogy (qiyas) and for urging it.

The majority of reciters read "nahnu qaddarna" with a shadda on the dal, and Kuthayyir alone read "nahnu qadarna" with the dal lightened. The meaning in both may be: We decreed and established; and it may mean: We made equal and ordered the earlier and later, that is, We made death into ranks, so the world does not die all at once, but in an order that no one escapes. Al-Tabari said: the meaning of the verse is: We decreed death among you on the condition that We replace your likenesses, that is, a group dies and We replace it with another group, generation after generation. His, the Exalted's, saying: "and We are not to be outdone" in replacing you, if We wish it, and in producing you in attributes that your deeds do not reach and your thoughts do not encompass. Al-Hasan said: [this refers to] your being transformed into apes and swine.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Hasan interpreted this because the verse tends toward warning, and the word "sabq" here comes in the manner of His, may blessings and peace be upon him, saying: "If you are able not to be overcome in the prayer before the rising of the sun and the prayer before its setting, then do so; do not let them escape you."

The majority of people read "al-nash'ah" with a sukun on the shin. Qatadah, Abu al-Ashhab, and Abu 'Amr in one report read "al-nash'ah" with a fatha and with the long vowel. Most exegetes said: it points to the creation of Adam and stopped on it, because you will not find anyone who denies that he is from the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, and that he is from clay. Some said: by "the first creation" he meant the creation of a human in childhood, so a person knows his own creation by what he sees of the creation of others.

Then the Exalted urged remembrance and reflection that leads to faith. The majority read "fa-lawla tadhakkarun" with a shadda on the dhal, and Talha read "fa-lawla tadhkurun" with a sukun on the dhal and a damma on the kaf. This verse is a clear text for the use of analogy (qiyas) and for urging it.

Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, says:

﴿Have you considered what you sow?﴾ ﴿Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could make it into crumbled debris, and you would be left amazed﴾ ﴿"Indeed, we are burdened with debt!"﴾ ﴿"Rather, we have been deprived!"﴾ ﴿Have you considered the water that you drink?﴾ ﴿Is it you who send it down from the clouds, or are We the sender?﴾ ﴿If We willed, We could make it bitter, so why do you not give thanks?﴾ ﴿Have you considered the fire that you kindle?﴾ ﴿Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producer?﴾ ﴿We made it a reminder and a provision for the travellers in the wilderness.﴾ ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾

Allah, the Exalted, questioned the disbelievers about the matter of sowing, which is the foundation of livelihood, and He made clear to everyone of sound nature that the ploughing which stirs up the earth and splits the seed does not actually do anything to the growth of the crop. A person may be called a sower (zāri') and from this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"it pleases the sowers"﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. But the meaning of this verse is: "Is it you who make it grow to completion, or is it Us?" Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, transmitted this verse.

"Ḥuṭām" (debris): the dry, crumbled plant matter that is heading toward destruction, and from it the wreckage of this world (ḥuṭām al-dunyā) is likened. It was also said that the meaning is: a stalk with no grain in it. "Tafakkahūn" (you would be amazed): Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said its meaning is "you would be astonished." 'Ikrima said: "you would blame one another." al-Hasan said: "its meaning is 'you would be astonished'." Ibn Zayd said: "you would lament." All of this is an explanation that does not specifically pertain to the word itself. What specifically pertains to the word is that you would cast off fruit from yourselves, and it is joy and gladness. A man is "fakih" when he is cheerful in spirit and unconcerned with things. "Tafakkaha" is among the siblings of "taḥarraja" and "taḥawwaba."

The majority read "fa-ẓaltum" with a fatḥa on the ẓā'. Sufyan al-Thawri transmitted, in the reading of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), a kasra on the ẓā'. Abu Hatim said: the vowel of the deleted lām was transferred onto it, and that is weak by analogy. This is the reading of Abu Haywa. Ahmad ibn Musa transmitted "fa-ẓallatum" with two lāms, the first with a fatḥa, from al-Jahdari, and it is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, with a kasra on the first lām.

As for the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"Indeed, we are burdened with debt!"﴾, before it there is an omitted element, estimated as "they say." al-A'mash and 'Asim al-Jahdari read "a'inna la-mughramūn" with two hamzas as an interrogative. The meaning may be: "Indeed, we are punished with torment (gharam)," and gharam is the most severe punishment. From it is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"Its punishment is ever-clinging torment (gharāman)"﴾ [al-Furqan: 65]. From it is also the verse of al-A'sha:

"If He punishes, it will be torment (gharam); and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."

It may also be that the meaning is: "Indeed, we are laden with a burden (gharam)," i.e., we have incurred expense and the loss of our crop. One says: "The man incurred debt (gharima), and I made him incur debt (aghramtuhu), so he is a debtor (mughram)." The explanation of "al-maḥrūm" was given earlier, and that it means the one cut off from provision and the one in want.

"Al-muzn": the clouds, without any disagreement. From it is the poet's saying:

"We are like the water of the clouds: in our possession there is nothing dull, nor is there among us anyone counted as a bargain for horses."

"Al-ujaj" is the most intensely salty of waters, and it is the water of the green sea. "Tūrūn" means: you strike sparks from the flint-sticks. One says: "I struck fire from the firestriker (zinād)." The zinād itself is reported, and the zinād may be made of two stones, or of a stone and an iron piece, or of wood, especially in the lands of the Arabs, for their firestrikers are of wood, particularly soft wood such as al-markh, al-'ifar, al-kalkh and what resembles them. Because it was the custom of the Arabs that their firestrikers were of wood, Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is it you who produced its tree?﴾. Some people of reflection said: by "the tree" He meant the fire itself, as if He, the Exalted, said: "its kind or its genus," and so He used "tree" metaphorically for that; this is a view with some strain. The majority read "a-antum" with a long vowel (madd), and it is transmitted from Abu 'Amr and 'Isa: "antum" without the madd, which Abu Hatim considered weak.

"Tadhkira" means: it reminds of the Fire of Hell, as said by Mujahid and Qatada. "Matā'" is what is benefited from. "Al-muqwīn" are those who are in a deserted place with weak things, like the saying of Ibn Zayd: "the fearful" and the like. Nothing stands for it except what we have mentioned. Whoever said its meaning is "the travellers" is close to what we have said, and this is the expression of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. One says: "aṣbaḥa al-rajul" (the man entered the morning), "aṣḥara" (he entered the open desert), and "aqwā" (he entered the empty land). From it: "aqwat al-dār, aqwā al-ṭalal," meaning it became empty (qiwā'). From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"...it became empty, and the ancient ages lingered upon it."

And the saying of another:

"...it became empty and desolate after Umm al-Haytham."

The poor and the rich are then alike in their need of fire, and nothing replaces its warmth in cold. Whoever said: "aqwā is among the antonyms, since it is said 'aqwā al-rajul' when his mount becomes strong," has erred; that is a different verb, like "atrab" when one becomes prosperous.

Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, commanded His Prophet to glorify his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and to exalt His beautiful names above what the disbelievers who argued in these verses say.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-Waqi'a, verses 75–87**

His, Exalted and Majestic is He, saying:

﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an.﴾ ﴿In a Book well-guarded.﴾ ﴿None touches it except the purified.﴾ ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Then is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it?﴾ ﴿So why not, when it [the soul] reaches the throat,﴾ ﴿and you, at that time, are looking on?﴾ ﴿And We are nearer to it than you, but you do not see.﴾ ﴿So why not, if you are not to be held to account,﴾ ﴿you return it [the soul], if you are truthful?﴾

The scholars differed concerning the "lā" in His saying, ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾. Some of the grammarians said: it is superfluous (zā'ida), and the meaning is "fa-uqsimu" ("so I swear"). Its superfluity in some places is well known, as in His saying, ﴿so that the People of the Scripture may know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], and other examples. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and some of the grammarians said: it is negating (nāfiya), as if He, exalted is He, were saying: "There is no truth in what the disbelievers say," and then the Blessed and Exalted One began and said: "Uqsimu" ("I swear"). Some of the interpreters said: it is emphatic (mu'akkida), giving intensification to the oath, and it is like opening a speech that resembles an oath with "allā" in common speech. From it is the saying of the poet:

*"Fa-lā wa-abī … lā akhūnuhā"*
("So, no, by my father … I shall not betray her")

The meaning is "fa-wa-abī" ("so, by my father"), i.e., her enemies. There are similar examples to this.

al-Hasan and al-Thaqafi read "fa-l'uqsimu" without an alif. Abu al-Fath said: the estimated form is "fa-la-anā uqsimu" ("so indeed I swear").

The majority of the reciters read "bi-mawāqi'" in the plural. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, and the people of Kufa, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, read "bi-mawqi'" in the singular, and it is intended as plural. Examples of this are many, and from it is His saying, ﴿Indeed, the most hateful of voices is the voice of the donkeys﴾ [Luqman: 19]. It is plural in that every donkey has a particular voice, and singular in that all voices are one category.

The people differed concerning "al-nujūm" (the stars) here. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid and others said: they are the stars of the Qur'an, which were revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ). This is because it is reported that the Qur'an descended from the presence of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, on the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr) to the lowest heaven all at once. It was also said: to the House of Frequent Visitation (al-Bayt al-Ma'mur). Then after that it was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) in separated portions (nujūman muqatta'a) over a period of twenty years. This interpretation is supported by the return of the pronoun to the Qur'an in His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾, because its mention has not preceded except on this interpretation. Whoever does not adopt this interpretation says: the pronoun returns to the Qur'an even though no mention has preceded it, because of the fame of the matter and the clarity of the meaning, as in His saying, ﴿until it [the sun] was hidden by the veil﴾ [Sad: 32], and ﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾ [al-Rahman: 26], and other examples.

Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat said:

*"Resolve and strength are better than the ihdān (softness/compromise) and the fahha and the ha'…"*

("So, no, by my father … I shall not betray her")

al-Hasan and al-Thaqafi read "fa-l'uqsimu" without an alif. Abu al-Fath said: the estimated form is "fa-la-anā uqsimu" ("so indeed I swear").

It is plural in that every donkey has a particular voice, and singular in that all voices are one category.

*"She raised, and the son of the slave-woman of the city was raised in her lap, you see him on his hoe, doing his work (yatarakkal)."*

He meant: the son of a slave-woman who was owned, and he was a servant who served the vineyard. It has been said about the meaning of this verse: he meant a town-dwelling labourer, because the Bedouins in the desert do not know farming and vineyard work, so he attributed him to the city because he was one of its people. "Dīn" of the king is his rule and his authority. al-Farra' inclined to this meaning, and al-Naqqash mentioned it in full detail. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿you return it﴾ takes the place of the answers and explanations that the specifications require. And "idhā" in His saying, ﴿So why not when﴾, and the repeated "in" (if), some of the speech carries other parts of it, by brevity and abbreviation.
