His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾, is that upon which the oath falls, and He described it with nobility in the sense of affirming the attributes of praise for it and repelling the attributes of deficiency from it.

The interpreters differed concerning His saying, ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾, although they agreed that "al-maknūn" means "al-maṣūn" (protected/preserved). Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: it means the Book that is in the heaven. 'Ikrima said: it means the Torah and the Gospel. As if He, Exalted is He, said: "Indeed, it is a noble Book," mentioning its nobility and honour, "in a Book well-guarded." So the meaning of the verse, according to this view, is the appeal to the revealed books. This is like His saying, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 36]. Some interpreters said: it means the codices (maṣāḥif) of the Muslims, although they did not exist on the day the verse was revealed. So it is, according to this view, a report of the unseen, and similarly it is "in a Book preserved until the Day of Resurrection." What supports this is the word "touch" (mass), for it points to the codices, and it is a metaphor taken from the touching of the angels.

The people differed concerning the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾, and concerning its ruling. Some of those who said that the Well-Guarded Book is the one in the heaven said: "the purified" here are the angels. Qatada said: "As for you, [the one who touches it] is the polytheist, the impure, and the hypocrite." al-Tabari said: "the purified" are the angels, the prophets, peace be upon them, and whoever has no sin. According to this view, there is no ruling in the verse concerning touching the codex for the rest of the children of Adam.

Whoever said that it refers to the codices of the Muslims said: His saying, Exalted is He, "None touches it," is a report whose implication is a prohibition. The vowel on the "sīn" according to this view is an i'rāb vowel (a grammatical case-ending vowel, ḍammat i'rāb). Some of this group said: the statement is a prohibition, and the vowel on the "sīn" is a bina' vowel (a fixed, non-inflected vowel, ḍammat bināʼ). All of them said: so none of the children of Adam may touch the codex except one who is pure from disbelief, from major ritual impurity (janāba), and from minor ritual impurity (ḥadath aṣghar). Mālik said: [the codex] is not to be carried by one who is not pure, by its strap or on a cushion. In the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to 'Amr ibn Hazm: "None touches the Qur'an except the pure." Abu Hanifa and a group allowed the one in major impurity and the menstruating woman to touch it through a barrier, such as a cover and the like. Some scholars allowed touching it in a state of minor impurity and reciting it from memory, among them Ibn 'Abbas and 'Amir al-Sha'bi, especially for the teacher and the children. Some allowed the one in major impurity to recite it. All of this permission is only according to the view we have mentioned, that "the purified" are the angels, or according to observing the wording "touch." Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I do not touch the codex, but I recite the Qur'an."

The majority of people read "al-muṭahharūn" with a fatḥa on the ṭā' and a shadda on the hā'. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr, according to one of the two narrations from them, read "al-muṭahharūn" with a sukūn on the ṭā' and a fatḥa on the hā', lightly; this is the reading of 'Isa al-Thaqafi. Salman al-Farisi read "al-muṭahharūn" with a fatḥa on the ṭā' lightly and a kasra on the hā' with a shadda, meaning "those who purify themselves." It is also narrated from him with a shadda on both the ṭā' and the hā'. al-Hasan, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Awn, and Salman al-Farisi, according to one narration from him, read "al-muṭahharūn" meaning "al-mutaṭahhirūn" (those who purify themselves).

The view that "None touches it" is a prohibition is a weak view. This is because, if it is a report, it occupies the place of a qualifying attribute (ṣifa). His saying after that, "A revelation," is also a qualifying attribute. So if we make it a prohibition, it introduces a foreign meaning interposed between the attributes, and this is not good in the arrangement of speech. So reflect on this. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "mā yamassuhu" ("which none touches"). This strengthens what I have preferred from the report, whose meaning is: its right and its worth is that none touches it except one who is pure.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then is it this discourse that you are scornful of?﴾ is addressed to the disbelievers. The "discourse" referred to is the Qur'an, which includes the resurrection, that Allah, Exalted is He, is the Creator of all things, that the son of Adam is directed by His decree and judgment, and other matters. "Mudhinūn" (scornful) means: some of you are soft toward one another and follow each other in disbelief. It is derived from "al-duhn" (oil), for its softness and smoothness. Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat said:

*"Resolve and strength are better than the ihdān (softness/compromise) and the fahha and the ha'…"*

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it is "al-muhawada" (yielding) in what is not lawful, and "al-mudara" (accommodation) is "al-muhawada" in what is lawful. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: "mudhinūn" means "mukadhdhibūn" (those who deny).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it?﴾ The exegetes agreed that the verse is a rebuke to those who said, concerning the rain that Allah, Exalted is He, sent down as provision for the servants: "This is due to the star-setting of such-and-such," and "This is due to the star-setting of the Lion," and "This is due to the star-setting of the Gemini," and other such things. The meaning is: "And you make the thanks for your provision," just as you say to a man: "You have made, O so-and-so, my kindness to you [into] that you insult me," meaning: "You made the thanks for my kindness." al-Haythan ibn 'Adi related that among the dialect of the Azd Shanu'a is: "What is the rizq of so-and-so?" meaning: "What is his shukr (thanks)?" 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, used to read it: "And you make your thanks that you deny," and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read likewise. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), except that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, put a ḍamma on the tā' and a fatḥa on the kāf, while 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, put a fatḥa on the tā', sukūn on the kāf, and lightened the dhāl. From this meaning is the saying of the poet:

*"The thanks of the people at the time of favours was the cauterizing of the healthy and the gouging of the eyes."*

Allah, Exalted is He, has informed that He sent down from the sky blessed water, and with it He produced gardens and the grain of the harvest, and tall palm trees with spathes stacked in layers, as provision for the servants. So this is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that you deny﴾, i.e., this report. 'Asim, in the narration of al-Mufaddal from him, read "tukadhdhibūn" with a fatḥa on the tā', sukūn on the kāf, and a lightened dhāl, like the reading of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him. Their lying in their statement is clear, because they say: "This is due to the star-setting of such-and-such," and that is a lie and fabrication from them.

al-Tabari mentioned that "the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, heard a man say: 'We were given rain by some of the clouds of the Lion,' so he said to him: 'You lie! Rather, it is the provision of Allah.'" The forbidden and disliked matter is that one believes the rising star has an influence on the rain. As for observing some of the risings according to the customary course, 'Umar said to al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, when they were seeking rain: "O 'Abbas, O uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ): How much of the nawʼ (star-rising) of the Pleiades remains?" al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The scholars say that it crosses the horizon seven [nights] after its setting." Ibn al-Musayyib said: "Seven had not passed until they were given rain."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So why not, when it [the soul] reaches the throat﴾, is a reproach upon a point of helplessness, which the consideration of it requires, that Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, is the Owner of everything. The pronoun in "reaches the throat" refers to the person himself, and the meaning requires it even though no mention of it has preceded. "Al-ḥulqūm" is the passage of food. This state is the person's struggle with death. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and you﴾, is an indication to all of mankind, and this is abbreviation (iqtiḍāb), like His saying, ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29]. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "ḥīnaʼidhin" with a kasra on the nūn. "Tanzurūn" means: looking at the one who struggles with death.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We are nearer to it than you﴾, may mean His angels and messengers, and it may mean: by Our power and Our dominion. According to the first possibility, His saying, ﴿but you do not see﴾, is from looking with the eye. According to the second interpretation, it is from looking with the heart. 'Amir ibn 'Abd Qays said: "I have not looked at anything except that I saw Allah, Exalted is He, nearer to it than myself."

Then the reproach and affirmation returned a second time with the wording of urging (taḥḍīḍ): "So why not, if you are not to be held to account." "Al-madīn" means "the owned (mamlūk)." This is the most correct thing said about the meaning of the word here. Whoever interpreted it as "one who is requited" or "one who is reckoned" has here an awkwardness, for the owned person turns the owner as he wishes. From this sense of ownership is the saying of al-Akhtal:

*"She raised, and the son of the slave-woman of the city was raised in her lap, you see him on his hoe, doing his work (yatarakkal)."*

He meant: the son of a slave-woman who was owned, and he was a servant who served the vineyard. It has been said about the meaning of this verse: he meant a town-dwelling labourer, because the Bedouins in the desert do not know farming and vineyard work, so he attributed him to the city because he was one of its people. So the meaning of the verse is: "So why do you not return the soul that has reached the throat, if you are not owned and not subjugated?" "Dīn" of the king is his rule and his authority. al-Farra' inclined to this meaning, and al-Naqqash mentioned it in full detail. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿you return it﴾ takes the place of the answers and explanations that the specifications require. And "idhā" in His saying, ﴿So why not when﴾, and the repeated "in" (if), some of the speech carries other parts of it, by brevity and abbreviation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 56, verses 88–96:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Then, if he is among those brought near (to Allah),﴾ ﴿there will be rest and sweet provision and a Garden of bliss.﴾ ﴿And if he is among the companions of the right,﴾ ﴿then, "Peace be upon you," from the companions of the right.﴾ ﴿And as for one who is among the deniers, the astray,﴾ ﴿there is a welcome of scalding water﴾ ﴿and burning in Hellfire.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty.﴾ ﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great.﴾

Allah, may He be exalted, mentions in this verse the state of the three categories of spouses mentioned at the beginning of the surah, and the state of each person among them. As for the one who is among the foremost, the brought near, he will meet at his death "rawh" (rest) and "rayhan" (sweet provision). "Rawh" means mercy, ease, relief and joy, and from it comes "rawh Allah" (the mercy of Allah). "Rayhan" means what is pleasant, and it is a sign of bliss. Mujahid said: "Rayhan" means provision. Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "Rayhan" is the well-known plant of this world. The one brought near will meet a "rayhan" from the Garden. (p-215) Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and a large group recited "fa-rawwih" with a dammah on the ra'. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that his spirit departs in his "rayhan." Al-Dahhak said: "Rayhan" is rest.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Rayhan" is that to which souls are inclined. Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi) said: it is the tip of every plant with a pleasant fragrance, in which are the first buds of light. The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both: "They are my two rayhans of this world." Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"The peace of God, His rayhan, His mercy, and a heaven abundant with rain."

'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite 'fa-rawwih' with a dammah on the ra'."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then, "Peace be upon you," from the companions of the right﴾ is an expression that implies a whole category of praise and a quality of safety and attainment of a high rank. The meaning is that there is nothing in their situation but peace and deliverance from punishment. This is like when you praise a man and say: "As for so-and-so, you have had enough of him," or "his affair is sufficient for you." This implies a general praise of him that is not detailed. The explanations of the commentators have varied concerning His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾. Some people said the meaning is: it is said to him, "Safe for you, that you are among the companions of the right." Al-Tabari said the meaning is: "Peace be upon you, you are from the companions of the right." It was also said the meaning is: "Peace be upon you, O Muhammad," i.e., you see among them only safety from punishment. So this "ka" in "dhalika" is either for the Prophet (ﷺ), which is the more apparent, and then for every person who takes heed from his community, or it is for the one addressed among the companions of the right. Other than this, of what has been said, there is excessive strain.

"The deniers, the astray" are the disbelievers, the companions of the left and the ill-omened. "Nuzul" is the first thing presented to a guest. "Tasliyah" is that the fire touches them. "Jahim" is the greatest part of the fire and where it is piled up. When the division of their states was complete and the report was concluded with that, Allah, may He be exalted, affirmed the announcement by saying to His Prophet, Muhammad (ﷺ), in an address that brings his community in with him: "Indeed, this which I have informed you of is the true certainty." The annexation of "haqq" (truth) to "yaqin" (certainty) is an expression containing emphasis, because the two have one meaning. Some people went to the view that it is of the type of "dar al-akhirah" (the abode of the Hereafter) and "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque). A group of the skilled scholars went to the view that it is like when you say, about a matter you are emphasizing: "This is the certainty of certainty," or "the correctness of correctness," meaning it is the utmost correctness. This is the best of what has been said about it, because "dar al-akhirah" and what resembles it may be understood as supposing a thing to which the abode is attributed, described as "the last," and then you omit it and put the description in its place, as if you said: "the abode of the last return," or "the last creation," or "the last circle." Here this does not apply. Rather, it is an expression of emphasis, and the meaning of the emphasis is that this report is the very certainty and its reality.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ is an expression that implies a command to turn away from the sayings of the disbelievers and all the affairs of this world that are particular to it, and to turn toward the affairs of the Hereafter, the worship of Allah, the Exalted, and calling to Him. 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir narrated that when ﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Make it in your bowing (ruku')." Then when ﴿Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1] was revealed, he said: "Make it in your prostration (sujud)." It is possible that the meaning is: glorify Allah, the Exalted, by mentioning His beautiful names. Here "al-ism" (the name) is in the sense of a genus, i.e., "by the names of your Lord," and "al-'Azim" (the Most Great) is an attribute of Him. So it is as if He commanded him to glorify Him by His greatest name, even though it was not specified. This is supported and indicated by the connection with surah al-Hadid, whose beginning contains glorification and a number of the names of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The greatest name of Allah is present in six verses from the beginning of surah al-Hadid." So contemplate this, for it is from subtle reflection. And for Allah, the Exalted, in His Mighty Book are hidden matters that minds barely grasp.

The tafsir of surah [al-Waqi'ah] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

"Rawh" means mercy, ease, relief and joy, and from it comes "rawh Allah" (the mercy of Allah). "Rayhan" means what is pleasant, and it is a sign of bliss. Mujahid said: "Rayhan" means provision. Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "Rayhan" is the well-known plant of this world. The one brought near will meet a "rayhan" from the Garden. (p-215) Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and a large group recited "fa-rawwih" with a dammah on the ra'. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that his spirit departs in his "rayhan." Al-Dahhak said: "Rayhan" is rest.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Rayhan" is that to which souls are inclined. Al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi) said: it is the tip of every plant with a pleasant fragrance, in which are the first buds of light. The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both: "They are my two rayhans of this world." Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"The peace of God, His rayhan, His mercy, and a heaven abundant with rain."

'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite 'fa-rawwih' with a dammah on the ra'."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then, "Peace be upon you," from the companions of the right﴾ is an expression that implies a whole category of praise and a quality of safety and attainment of a high rank. The meaning is that there is nothing in their situation but peace and deliverance from punishment. This is like when you praise a man and say: "As for so-and-so, you have had enough of him," or "his affair is sufficient for you." This implies a general praise of him that is not detailed. The explanations of the commentators have varied concerning His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾. Some people said the meaning is: it is said to him, "Safe for you, that you are among the companions of the right." Al-Tabari said the meaning is: "Peace be upon you, you are from the companions of the right." It was also said the meaning is: "Peace be upon you, O Muhammad," i.e., you see among them only safety from punishment. So this "ka" in "dhalika" is either for the Prophet (ﷺ), which is the more apparent, and then for every person who takes heed from his community, or it is for the one addressed among the companions of the right. Other than this, of what has been said, there is excessive strain.

"The deniers, the astray" are the disbelievers, the companions of the left and the ill-omened. "Nuzul" is the first thing presented to a guest. "Tasliyah" is that the fire touches them. "Jahim" is the greatest part of the fire and where it is piled up. When the division of their states was complete and the report was concluded with that, Allah, may He be exalted, affirmed the announcement by saying to His Prophet, Muhammad (ﷺ), in an address that brings his community in with him: "Indeed, this which I have informed you of is the true certainty." The annexation of "haqq" (truth) to "yaqin" (certainty) is an expression containing emphasis, because the two have one meaning. Some people went to the view that it is of the type of "dar al-akhirah" (the abode of the Hereafter) and "masjid al-jami'" (the congregational mosque). A group of the skilled scholars went to the view that it is like when you say, about a matter you are emphasizing: "This is the certainty of certainty," or "the correctness of correctness," meaning it is the utmost correctness. This is the best of what has been said about it, because "dar al-akhirah" and what resembles it may be understood as supposing a thing to which the abode is attributed, described as "the last," and then you omit it and put the description in its place, as if you said: "the abode of the last return," or "the last creation," or "the last circle." Here this does not apply. Rather, it is an expression of emphasis, and the meaning of the emphasis is that this report is the very certainty and its reality.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ is an expression that implies a command to turn away from the sayings of the disbelievers and all the affairs of this world that are particular to it, and to turn toward the affairs of the Hereafter, the worship of Allah, the Exalted, and calling to Him. 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir narrated that when ﴿So exalt the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Make it in your bowing (ruku')." Then when ﴿Exalt the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1] was revealed, he said: "Make it in your prostration (sujud)." It is possible that the meaning is: glorify Allah, the Exalted, by mentioning His beautiful names. Here "al-ism" (the name) is in the sense of a genus, i.e., "by the names of your Lord," and "al-'Azim" (the Most Great) is an attribute of Him. So it is as if He commanded him to glorify Him by His greatest name, even though it was not specified. This is supported and indicated by the connection with surah al-Hadid, whose beginning contains glorification and a number of the names of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The greatest name of Allah is present in six verses from the beginning of surah al-Hadid." So contemplate this, for it is from subtle reflection. And for Allah, the Exalted, in His Mighty Book are hidden matters that minds barely grasp.

The tafsir of surah [al-Waqi'ah] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
